clue.text: Moderate a medium

parts.note: to moderate something is to temper it, tone it down

explanation.surface: An instruction to tone down a spiritualist medium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Medium' suggests a psychic, but it is the painter's sense: a substance pigment is mixed with.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempera is a painting medium in which pigment is bound with egg yolk.

clue.text: Set aside gospel on organ

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting on another means it comes first, above it

parts.note: the ear is the organ of hearing
Mark is one of the four Gospels of the New Testament

explanation.surface: Someone sets aside a gospel text to place on a church organ.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' points to church music, but it is the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: To earmark funds is to reserve them for a particular purpose.

clue.text: Very good female characters by Pym

definitions.meaning: Barbara Pym's 1952 novel ... Women names its spinster heroines with this adjective

explanation.surface: A verdict that Barbara Pym's women characters are very well drawn.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a literary-quiz cue: Pym's novel title is the answer plus 'Women', so the answer is the word describing her female characters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something outstanding or first-rate is very good indeed.

clue.text: Dramatist takes vestment with ease, by the sound of it

parts.note: an alb is a white linen vestment worn by priests

indicators.note: tells us the word ease is to be taken for how it is said, as the letter name E twice

parts.note: the word ease said aloud sounds like 'E's', two letter Es

explanation.surface: A playwright slips into a priest's robe comfortably.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, 'ease' is 'Es': the letter E twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Albee was the American playwright of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?

clue.text: One providing subject matter for John Berryman's 1972 verse?

definitions.text: One providing subject matter for John Berryman's 1972 verse?

parts.words: One providing subject matter for John Berryman's 1972 verse
parts.note: Berryman's 1972 collection is Delusions, Etc.; whoever plants false beliefs would supply its subject

explanation.surface: A question about who inspired a late book of Berryman's poems.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet's 1972 book is Delusions, Etc., so the supplier of its subject is someone who misleads.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who leads others into false beliefs is a deceiver, the source of delusions.

clue.text: Hera led moves to describe sort of wreath

indicators.note: the letters of the goddess's name and the verb are moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: The goddess Hera leads a procession wearing a ceremonial garland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moves' rearranges HERALED (Hera led).
explanation.definitionFit: Hederal means relating to ivy, from Latin hedera, so a hederal wreath is an ivy garland.

clue.text: One act of Shaffer in view of all

definitions.meaning: Peter Shaffer wrote a one-act play of this name (1962), paired with The Private Ear
being seen and noticed by everyone, as a celebrity is

explanation.surface: A scene from a Shaffer play performed before everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One act' looks like a single scene, but it describes a one-act play.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in the public eye is to be watched and talked about by people at large.

clue.text: Big hit in charge of epic style

parts.note: a home run in baseball is called a homer

explanation.surface: A slugger's huge blow takes command in the grand manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Homeric describes the grand heroic manner of the Iliad and Odyssey, the archetypal epics.

clue.text: Clip concerning Sapper's protagonist

definitions.meaning: a strong spring clip for holding papers together
Sapper (H. C. McNeile) wrote the ... Drummond adventure novels

explanation.surface: A news clip about the hero of a thriller writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Sapper was the pen name of H. C. McNeile, whose hero is Captain Hugh 'Bulldog' Drummond.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulldog clip is a sprung metal stationery clip, and Bulldog is Drummond's nickname.

clue.text: Scott character ridiculing concealed fashion

indicators.note: says one word is hidden away inside the other

parts.note: to guy someone is to mock them, so ridiculing is guying
a manner is a way or fashion of doing something

explanation.surface: A Walter Scott figure mocks a hidden trend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' as a verb (to mock) is a British usage from Guy Fawkes effigies; 'concealed' is the container signal, with the fashion word held within.
explanation.definitionFit: Guy Mannering is the title hero of Walter Scott's 1815 novel.

clue.text: Have the edge, like new Lear VIP

indicators.note: a new version of these letters is a reshuffled arrangement

explanation.surface: Winning out, like a fresh King Lear star performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges LEARVIP.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevail is to win through or come out on top.

clue.text: "Mr Salteena was an ——' man of forty two…" (Daisy Ashford)

definitions.text: "Mr Salteena was an ——' man of forty two…" (Daisy Ashford)

parts.words: "Mr Salteena was an ——' man of forty two…" (Daisy Ashford)
parts.note: the opening line of The Young Visiters, written by the nine-year-old Daisy Ashford, with the word for a man getting on in years left blank

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from The Young Visiters.
explanation.walkthrough: Ashford wrote the novel as a child, which is why forty-two counts as old.
explanation.definitionFit: A child's view of a man of forty-two as getting on in years, aged.

clue.text: Read Salem version of wrongly accused witch

indicators.note: a version of these words is the same letters in another arrangement

explanation.surface: A reading of the Salem story about an innocent woman tried as a witch.
explanation.walkthrough: Salem points to the 1692 witch trials, but the witch is Hugo's: 'version of' rearranges READSALEM.
explanation.definitionFit: Esmeralda, the gypsy dancer in Hugo's Notre-Dame de Paris, is falsely tried for witchcraft.

clue.text: Christine Brooke-Rose's multiple version of The Go-Between?

definitions.text: Christine Brooke-Rose's multiple version of The Go-Between?

parts.words: Christine Brooke-Rose's multiple version of The Go-Between
parts.note: L. P. Hartley's title names a single intermediary; Brooke-Rose's 1961 satirical novel is titled with the plural of a synonym

explanation.surface: A question casting a Brooke-Rose novel as a plural remake of Hartley's.
explanation.walkthrough: Brooke-Rose wrote The Middlemen: A Satire (1961); a go-between is an intermediary, and her title is plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Intermediaries who pass goods or messages between two parties are go-betweens in the plural.

clue.text: Apparent claim of any book, having gone through learning process

definitions.meaning: a book seems to declare it was printed, bearing its publisher's imprint
young animals bond to a parent figure in an early fixed learning stage

explanation.surface: A book's boast that its reader has been educated.
explanation.walkthrough: Imprinting is the term from animal behaviour for the rapid attachment learning of newborns, as Lorenz's goslings to him.
explanation.definitionFit: Printed with an imprint, and bonded through the ethologists' early attachment learning.

clue.text: Nell Dunn work in which the indigent subdue

parts.note: indigent people are the poor
to cow is to intimidate into submission

explanation.surface: A novel in which poverty-stricken people are kept down.
explanation.definitionFit: Poor Cow is Nell Dunn's 1967 novel of a young London mother, filmed by Ken Loach.

clue.text: First illuminated in early MS .

definitions.meaning: the large decorated opening capital painted in a medieval manuscript

explanation.surface: The earliest thing lit up in an old handwritten book.
explanation.walkthrough: MS is the abbreviation for manuscript; the illuminated capital of a medieval page is its opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An initial is the opening letter, and as an adjective it means earliest.

clue.text: Support for Jacobean board extension

parts.note: the hinged swing-out leg that holds up a drop leaf on a seventeenth-century table

explanation.surface: Something propping up an extension on old furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' is an old word for a table; such drop-leaf tables were popular in Jacobean England.
explanation.definitionFit: A swinging leg built like a gate props the hinged leaf of a drop-leaf table.

clue.text: Spice it liberally with heroic efforts he makes

indicators.note: applying the words liberally scatters their letters into a free arrangement

explanation.surface: A cook seasons generously, putting real effort in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberally' rearranges SPICEIT; the definition reads as 'he makes heroic efforts', i.e. epics.
explanation.definitionFit: An epicist writes epics, long heroic poems, so his efforts are heroic works.

clue.text: Elegies of Propertius (discreetly available in back room?)

definitions.text: Elegies of Propertius (discreetly available in back room?)

parts.words: Elegies of Propertius (discreetly available in back room
parts.note: the Roman poet's love poems, with the bookseller's back room where racy material was kept

explanation.surface: Classical love poems sold under the counter.
explanation.walkthrough: Propertius wrote passionate love elegies to Cynthia; the back room is where shops kept saucy books.
explanation.definitionFit: Literature or art concerned with sexual love, such as amorous Latin elegies.

clue.text: Slang for old wool-ship on time

indicators.note: here the piece for time is added on after the ship

parts.note: the Argo carried Jason in quest of the Golden Fleece

explanation.surface: A word for vernacular talk aboard an old vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'wool' is the Golden Fleece Jason's Argo sailed for.
explanation.definitionFit: Argot is the jargon or cant of a particular group.

clue.text: Reformer conceals one instrument maker

indicators.note: the reformer's name keeps the other piece hidden inside it

parts.note: Martin Luther led the Protestant Reformation
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A Protestant reformer is secretly a craftsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A luthier makes stringed instruments such as violins and lutes.

clue.text: Applying the acid test to art?

definitions.text: Applying the acid test to art?

parts.words: Applying the acid test to art
parts.note: an acid test usually means a decisive trial, here literally biting a metal plate with acid to make a picture

explanation.surface: A critic putting artworks to a decisive trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acid test' is meant literally: printmakers bite their design into a metal plate with acid.
explanation.definitionFit: Printmaking in which acid bites lines into a metal plate.

clue.text: "We must be strangers; Nor would 1. have you seen here for a " (Massinger, A New Way To Pay Old Debts)

definitions.text: "We must be strangers; Nor would 1. have you seen here for a " (Massinger, A New Way To Pay Old Debts)

parts.words: "We must be strangers; Nor would 1. have you seen here for a " (Massinger, A New Way To Pay Old Debts)
parts.note: a line of Massinger's comedy ending on a blank for a huge number, i.e. not at any price

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank line from a Jacobean comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The '1.' is the printed I; 'not for a million' means not for any reward.
explanation.definitionFit: A thousand thousand, used for any vast sum one would refuse.

clue.text: Shakespeare's epiphany?

parts.note: a sudden revelation by the playwright, or the feast of Epiphany as he titled a comedy

explanation.surface: A moment of sudden insight for the Bard.
explanation.walkthrough: Epiphany, 6 January, is the evening after the twelve days of Christmas, and a Shakespeare comedy bears that name.
explanation.definitionFit: The eve of the Epiphany, the last night of the Christmas season.
